zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: the supplied subset of Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510 (CC BY 4.0), was consulted after independent scan reading. Release: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html . These diplomatic readings and comments are the reviewer's scan-based work, not a reproduction of the lexical dataset.

lines.note: Gongo denotes words or speech. The example begins gongoni oyobanu, something beyond verbal expression; the scan's initial G replaces OCR C. The printed hyphen belongs to voyoba-.
Nu completes oyobanu; noberarenu offers the alternative “cannot be expressed.” The Portuguese begins the corresponding explanation, “cannot be explained.”

The first translation ends “with words.” Gongo wo zessuru then describes words failing to convey something. The short mark in Gõgo is retained as a nasal abbreviation, rather than the draft's long-o caron; its impression is weak. Pa continues as lauras without a supplied hyphen.

Lauras completes palauras: lacking words to praise or emphasize something. The next expression is gongododan, continued below; its nasal abbreviation and the distinct caron over the later o are kept separately.

Dã completes gongododan. The repeated Japanese gloss explains it as being beyond words, followed by italic Idẽ, “the same.” The abbreviated nasal marks are faint but compatible with this reading; the OCR's Ioẽ is not supported by the surviving d.

runs.text: que ſe ẽcarece algũa couſa em bem, ou mal.

lines.note: The phrase can emphasize something either favorably or unfavorably. This qualification belongs to gongododan and should not be narrowed to its modern predominantly condemnatory use.
Gongo shindai pairs speech with bodily action; the Portuguese explicitly gives “words and deeds.” It is a separate entry, not a continuation of the preceding evaluation.

Gongyo is explained by tsutome and okonau, performing religious exercises or observances. The Portuguese calls these good exercises; the printed Japanese spellings and the abbreviated bõs remain unchanged.
Gonichi is a later day or future occasion, paraphrased nochi no hi. The Portuguese definition starts with “time to come.”
The first gloss continues “time ahead.” Gonichi no tame ni mosu means saying something for future reference, which the next line translates.

runs.text: Digo, ou falo pera odiante, ou tempo futuro.

lines.note: This translates the preceding example as speaking for the future. The historical spacing odiante and spelling pera are preserved rather than normalized.

Gonin here is a person who commits evil deeds, as akugo wo nasu hito makes explicit. Its circumflex distinguishes it graphically from the subsequent Gǒnin entry; per continues into the next row without an added hyphen.
Uerso completes perverso. The example refers to an evildoer burdened with grave offenses; Giǔzai retains the printed historical spelling and its caron.
The example's translation is a wicked person with many evil deeds. It completes the criminal or karmic sense, before the separate territorial entry below.
Gǒnin denotes a person or people of a district. The definition continues with their rising in revolt; the visible caron is not the preceding entry's circumflex.

runs.text: ou territorio que ſe aleuanta, ou amutina.

lines.note: The district's inhabitants rise or mutiny. This relative clause completes the definition and anticipates the explicit example on the following row.
Gonin ga okoru illustrates the local people's uprising. The damaged initial group reads Goninga, not Groninga; no additional long-vowel mark is supplied where the impression does not establish one.

runs.text: narſe a gẽte de hũa parte do reino, ou comarca.

lines.note: Narſe completes amutinarſe, describing rebellion by people in one part of a kingdom or district. The two nasal abbreviations remain unexpanded.

runs.text: Goninbari. i, Gonin faru fodono yumi.

lines.note: Goninbari is a bow requiring the strength of five people to bend or string. The Japanese explanation is gonin haru hodo no yumi.
The Portuguese confirms a bow strung by five men. The example begins Gonin- and continues on the next physical row.
Bari no yumi completes the compound example for the same five-man bow. Idem refers to the preceding definition.
Gonja is characterized as outstanding in learning and virtue. The definition's religious dimension becomes explicit in the continuation.

runs.text: tude, & zeloſo da ſaluação dos outros.

lines.note: Tude completes virtude; the person is also zealous for others' salvation. This is the dictionary's own religious explanation, not a new entry.
Gonjet, with a retained final t, denotes verbal expression and is paraphrased by kotoba and shita. The example begins the abbreviated Gõ-, whose small nasal mark differs from a clear long-o caron.
Jetni completes gonjet ni oyobanu: not expressible in words. The Portuguese translation begins “cannot be explained.”
“With words” completes the preceding example's translation. This short line remains independently represented.
The second Gonjet entry means explaining through words: kotoba wo motte toku. The Portuguese gives preaching, with speaking added below.
“Or speaking” completes the second Gonjet definition, distinguishing an activity from the preceding entry's words or expression.
Gonjiqi concerns ornament or splendor; kazari and kazaru supply Japanese equivalents. The Portuguese luſtre is retained with its draft allograph rather than globally regularized.
Gonjo is deferentially addressing a noble person, paraphrased moshi aguru. The scan establishes Gonjǒ rather than OCR Cionjǒ.
Gonjo tsukamatsuru and gonjo toguru are alternative expressions for making such a respectful address. Vt is italic; the Japanese forms and alternative marker remain roman.
This separate Gonjo entry concerns adornment and beauty, not addressing a superior. Qi- starts the illustrative qirei gonjo phrase below.
Rei completes qirei, yielding qirei gonjo for beautiful adornment. Idem points to the preceding ornament-and-beauty definition.
Gono is an honored person's illness, explained here specifically as the king's illness. Von nayami retains its printed honorific spelling.
Goppo is recompense for deeds, paraphrased shiwaza no mukui. The Portuguese begins “retribution for the works,” continued below.

The main text completes recompense for the deeds one does. At the far right the scan also prints a parenthesis-like mark and q̃ fez, omitted by OCR. This displaced phrase completes the next entry's “evils that he did”; it remains at its actual printed height rather than being moved into that sentence.
Gopponin is a person punished for evil deeds. Its completion q̃ fez is printed above at the far right of c1-l036, where it has been restored; no new physical row is invented.

Goke is a widow, literally a woman surviving her husband. The short, sloping mark over võna is read as a damaged nasal abbreviation for onna rather than a long-o caron; its exact shape is not fully secure. The gloss ends with a period.
Gokeiri denotes a widow's marriage to a new husband. The damaged capital is G, and the Portuguese reads com, not OCR cem.

runs.text: homem, q̃ ſoccede na caſa do primeiro marido.

lines.note: The new husband succeeds to the first husband's household. This qualification is essential to the entry's meaning, beyond merely a widow remarrying.

runs.text: Eſcudela de pao ẽ que ſe come o arroz.

lines.note: Goki is a wooden bowl used for eating rice. The Portuguese nasal abbreviation ẽ is kept without expansion.
This separate Goki means five demons, explicitly itsutsu no oni. The following rows recount their subjugation and a related mountain-pilgrimage practice.

runs.text: quais hum Yamabuxi por nome Yenno guiǒja

lines.note: The relative clause names the yamabushi En no Gyoja as the person who subdued them. Yamabuxi begins with Y, not OCR V; the mark in guiǒja is a caron. These embedded Japanese designations are retained in the locally italic explanation.

runs.text: venceo, & ſujeitou, & agora em lugar des-

lines.note: The named ascetic conquered and subjected the demons. The account then turns to people appearing in their place; des- continues as tes below.

runs.text: tes aparecem là na ſerra que ſe diz Vonmine,

lines.note: Tes completes destes. The account says that in their place others appear on the mountain called Vonmine. The first e of aparecem is almost lost: tiny ink remnants occupy its position, and the surrounding Portuguese supports this supplied reading. It remains a nonblocking damaged-letter uncertainty, not a clearly intact glyph. Vonmine is an embedded Japanese mountain name.

runs.text: cinco homẽs veſtidos de cinco cores que ſaem

lines.note: Five men wearing five colors emerge in place of the demons. The line continues the historical account, rather than defining another sense of Goqi.

runs.text: ao encontro aos Yamabuxis que vão à ſerra em

lines.note: These men meet the yamabushi traveling to the mountain. The embedded plural Yamabuxis belongs within the Portuguese sentence and is a typeface-review candidate.
Romaria completes the description of a pilgrimage. The short line is body text above the lower rule, not a catchword.
Gokiganjo is a place for prayers or petitions. The Portuguese identifies it as a temple built by royal initiative; Te- continues into ra.

runs.text: ra que o Rei fez, ou mandou aleuantar.

lines.note: Ra completes Tera, a temple made or ordered built by the king. The initial syllable is kept on the preceding physical row.
Gokyo is defined as five books, itsutsu no hon, of China. The capital is visibly G, correcting OCR C; Chi- continues into na.

runs.text: na que tratão das couſas moraes. V. G.

lines.note: The five Chinese books concern moral matters. V. G. introduces the following list and is printed in the same italic apparatus, rather than with an isolated roman G.
This row lists the titles as Yeqi, raiqi, môxi, jǒjo, and xunju. The scan's circumflex in môxi replaces the draft's caron; the list is retained literally rather than adjusted to an expected canon.
Goraku means pleasure or enjoyment, with tanoshimi and raku as equivalents. The second equivalent begins with the clear R of Racu, not OCR Bacu.
Res completes prazeres. Tenjo no goraku illustrates heavenly delights, translated by contentamentos across this line and the next.
This completes “the delights of heaven.” Ceo is the printed historical Portuguese spelling, not an error to modernize.
Goran is honorific seeing, used when the person doing the seeing is noble. The example begins goran aru, not a command to look at a noble person.
Ru completes aru; nasaruru supplies the alternative honorific predicate. The whole row belongs to the example introduced above.
Goranji gives principal forms of the honorific verb for seeing. The Portuguese again specifies a noble subject, and the historical endings are preserved.
Goranji okurare describes respectfully watching someone depart. The scan supports vocurare rather than OCR vocurate; the noble observer is identified in the continuation.

runs.text: nobre a companhando com a viſta ao q̃ ſe vai.

lines.note: A noble person follows the departing person with their gaze. The printed separation a companhando is retained rather than silently normalized to acompanhando.
Gorei here is customary precedent, tsune no tameshi, not an order or command. The Portuguese begins “ordinary custom.”
Rio completes ordinario; como foro likens the custom to an established practice or customary obligation.
Gorenchu denotes a noble lady or the wife of a yakata. Yacata is a Japanese designation embedded in the Portuguese gloss, whose typography is kept italic here.
The wife may be that of a great tono, or lord. Tono is another Japanese designation embedded in the explanatory Portuguese.
Goreonin respectfully denotes a daughter, initially specified as a noble person's daughter by kinin no musume. The scope is broadened below.

runs.text: peßoa nobre, ou de outra ſomenos falando

lines.note: The expression can also refer to the daughter of someone of lower rank, provided that one speaks respectfully. Somenos carries that comparative social qualification.
“With honor” completes the usage qualification. It explains why the designation is not restricted absolutely to noble birth.

runs.text: Renda que eſta encabeçada na co-

lines.note: Goreosho concerns revenue assigned to the crown. The headword begins with G, not OCR C; the visibly unaccented eſta is retained.

runs.text: roa, ou renda, & terras particulares do Rey.

lines.note: Roa completes coroa; the alternative explanation is the king's own revenue and lands. Both descriptions belong to the same entry.
This Gori is a shellfish term, glossed by repeated hamaguri and Portuguese ameijoas. The repetition is printed and is not removed as redundant.
As completes ameijoas, specifying clams of the shore. Praya retains its historical y spelling.
This distinct plant term is called karasuuri in the Cami region. Caraſuuri is visibly roman inside the italic explanation; Cami is an embedded regional designation.

runs.text: fruita como melonzinhos, que nacem de

lines.note: The fruit resembles little melons growing from a plant. The source's fruita and nacem are retained, rather than modernized.
The printed era completes the plant description where erva would be expected semantically. No intervening v is securely visible, so the apparent source anomaly is retained.
Gorimekashi gives forms for making a crunching sound with the teeth. The Portuguese specifies the circumstances in the next two rows.

runs.text: dentes quando ſe come couſa verde, ou dura

lines.note: The sound arises while eating something green or hard. This is a description of chewing or crunching, not speech.
Chestnuts provide the example of hard food. The draft's st representation is retained under the supplied policy for ambiguous italic st ligatures.
Gorimeki gives the related crunching action. The Portuguese trincar describes biting the green or hard item between the teeth.
“And so on, in the teeth” completes the chewing definition. The abbreviated continuation remains a separate physical line.

runs.text: Gorin. Facano vyeni tatçuru xiruxino ixi.

lines.note: Gorin is explained as a marker stone erected above a grave: haka no ue ni tatsuru shirushi no ishi. The spelling vyeni is retained.

runs.text: Pedras que ſe poem por ſinal em cima das co-

lines.note: The Portuguese describes stones placed as markers over graves. Co- begins covas at the physical line ending.
Uas completes covas dos defuntos, the graves of the dead, compared with tombstones or slabs. No additional monument terminology is inserted.
Goriki here is a yamabushi's attendant or servant, as yamabushi no komono explains. Portuguese Moço corrects OCR Meço.
“Servant of a yamabushi” completes the definition. Yamabuxi is embedded in the Portuguese explanation and appears in its italic type.
This second Goriki means great physical strength, tsuyoi chikara. It is distinct from the preceding attendant sense.
Gorikina mono ja says that someone is a strong person. The scan contains a pilcrow before the example, absent from the draft; grã- continues the Portuguese adjective below.
Des completes grandes forças, “great strength.” The visible o in forças corrects OCR ferças.

runs.text: Forçoſo, ou homẽ de grandes forças.

lines.note: Gorikisha denotes a powerful or strong person. Both Portuguese formulations explicitly describe strength, not a different occupation.
Goro is five kinds of fatigue, paraphrased itsutsu no tsukare. The weak accent is retained as the draft's caron.
The five kinds are of tiredness or weakness. Final S. is an upright usage label for written language, not part of the italic definition.
Goroku means large stones. The example begins with the stones as the object, goroku wo, and continues with verbs of dropping or throwing.
Otoshikakuru and naguru are alternatives for casting these stones. The Portuguese translation begins here and specifies their military use below.

runs.text: pedras da fortaleza ſobre os inimigos.

lines.note: The stones are thrown down from the fortress onto enemies. This completes the example, not an independent definition.
This separate Goroku is a book of authoritative sayings associated with the Zen sect, represented by printed Ienxus. That embedded designation is not modernized in the transcription.
